evaluation.positioning_hook: A grieving Catholic brother and his cop sister are pulled into a blood feud with a sadistic crime family, forcing them to choose between vengeance, justice, and what’s left of their faith.

audience_appeal_marketability.reasoning: The emotional engine is clear and the crime-family revenge spine is easy to sell, but the script’s intensity, religious specificity, and punishing body count narrow the audience. It feels built for adult thriller/drama buyers more than broad theatrical play.

conceptual_hook_clarity.reasoning: The hook lands early: a devastated brother, a cop sister, and a criminal family tied to a massacre. The opening is dense and the family tree takes a minute to fully orient, but the central conflict is legible.

character_appeal_and_long_term_potential.reasoning: Jacob and Jodie both have strong emotional engines, and Ethan gives the script a morally conflicted third point of view. Victor is a vivid antagonist, though several of the Risaldi brothers function more as variations on menace than fully separate personalities.

creative_originality_and_boldness.reasoning: The Catholic confession framework, the recurring prayer/music motifs, and the way grief is staged through ritual give the script a distinct identity. The underlying revenge-crime structure is familiar, but the spiritual register makes it feel authored.

narrative_momentum_engagement.reasoning: The script keeps moving through reversals, raids, betrayals, and escalating confrontations, with the club and mansion sequences giving it real propulsion. Some transitions are exposition-heavy, but the final act is built to keep pressure on every character.

resonant_originality.reasoning: The premise is recognizable but the combination of Catholic guilt, family annihilation, and organized-crime reckoning gives it a fresh emotional signature. The opening massacre and the confession-booth framing make the story immediately ownable.

world_density_and_texture.reasoning: The police station, church, mansion, club, docks, and family home all feel like parts of a lived-in civic ecosystem. The Risaldi hierarchy and the city’s public response suggest a broader world beyond the immediate plot.

tonal_specificity.reasoning: The script has a very specific tonal blend: devotional, operatic, and brutal, with prayer and violence constantly colliding. The repeated hymns, confessional scenes, and ritualized violence create a hard-to-mistake identity.

latent_depth_slow_burn_potential.reasoning: There’s real thematic depth around sin, absolution, inherited violence, and whether justice can ever cleanse grief. The script keeps returning to those ideas through Father Michael, Ethan, and Jodie, which gives it more resonance than a standard revenge piece.

relationship_density_and_ensemble_engine.reasoning: The Jacob/Jodie sibling bond, Ethan’s split loyalty, Victor’s control over his sons, and Father Michael’s pastoral role all generate recurring dramatic friction. Multiple pairings can carry scenes, and the family structure itself is story-generating.

lead_characters.name: Jacob Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 30s to early 40s, Catholic, working-class family man, grieving father and brother.
lead_characters.hook: Jacob is the emotional center of the film: a devout, soft-spoken family man whose faith is shattered by the murder of his wife and children, then weaponized by his need for meaning. He starts as the wounded survivor and becomes a man willing to cross moral lines while still believing he is pursuing justice.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the showcase territory of Casey Affleck in Manchester by the Sea — a grief-saturated role that lives in restraint, then detonates when the character finally breaks. It gives an actor the chance to play interior devastation, moral contradiction, and physical vengeance in the same performance.

lead_characters.name: Jodie Smith
lead_characters.demographics: Female, late 30s, police officer, Catholic, Jacob’s sister.
lead_characters.hook: Jodie is a workaholic cop trying to outrun grief by staying in motion, and the script keeps testing whether her professionalism is strength or avoidance. She is both Jacob’s anchor and his mirror: the sibling who wants justice, but not at the cost of becoming what she hunts.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gave Amy Adams in Sharp Objects or Regina King in If Beale Street Could Talk room to carry pain with authority — a woman whose competence is inseparable from her damage. It offers a strong actor the chance to play command, collapse, and sibling love without ever softening the edges.

lead_characters.name: Ethan Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 20s, Catholic, morally conflicted member of the Risaldi family.
lead_characters.hook: Ethan is the script’s conscience inside the enemy camp: principled, frightened, and desperate to believe he can still choose a different life. He’s not a clean hero, but he’s the rare family member who can see the machinery of violence and still reach for absolution.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of morally split, emotionally exposed role that made Michael Shannon in Take Shelter or Jesse Plemons in The Power of the Dog so compelling — a man whose stillness hides panic and conviction at once. It gives an actor a chance to play intelligence, shame, and spiritual yearning without losing tension.

lead_characters.name: Victor Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, late 60s, crime patriarch, authoritarian father.
lead_characters.hook: Victor is the engine of the family’s corruption: composed, cruel, and convinced that domination is the same thing as order. He treats his children like disposable instruments and speaks in the language of purpose, which makes him more chilling than a simple thug.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is prime Brian Cox in Succession territory — a patriarch role built on command, humiliation, and the ability to make every room feel smaller. It gives a veteran actor a monologue-heavy, power-drenched part with real menace and prestige weight.

lead_characters.name: Father Michael
lead_characters.hook: Father Michael is the film’s spiritual counterweight, a priest who speaks in parables, humor, and hard-earned compassion. He’s not just counseling grief; he’s trying to give the characters a framework for surviving guilt without surrendering to it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that lets an actor do what Paul Dano did in The Fabelmans or Mark Ruffalo in Spotlight — warmth, authority, and moral clarity without becoming a sermon. It offers a rich supporting turn with real emotional payoff and memorable dialogue.

lead_characters.name: Martin Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Martin is the family’s most volatile instrument: sadistic, theatrical, and deeply broken under the performance of control. He’s terrifying because he seems to enjoy the violence even as the script hints that he’s also trapped inside it.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of feral, prestige-villain role that lets an actor do what Jack Gleeson did with Joffrey or what Tom Hardy has done in his most unhinged work — charisma fused with cruelty. It’s a scene-stealing part with real volatility.

lead_characters.name: Edward Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Edward is the family’s blunt-force arm, a near-silent muscle piece whose loyalty is expressed through violence and obedience. He’s less psychologically articulated than Martin or Ethan, but he gives the family its physical threat level.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is strong character-actor or physical-performer territory, similar to the kind of role that gave Dave Bautista in Blade Runner 2049 or Michael Mando in Better Call Saul a chance to project danger with minimal dialogue. It’s a showcase for presence, intimidation, and controlled brutality.

lead_characters.name: Frankie Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Male, early 30s, family enforcer with a softer edge.
lead_characters.hook: Frankie is the family member most visibly split between loyalty and conscience, which makes him one of the script’s most tragic figures. He wants to be useful, wants to protect Ethan, and still ends up trapped in the same machinery as everyone else.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of role that gives an actor the emotional contradiction of a Michael Imperioli or a Ben Foster part — dangerous, wounded, and capable of sudden collapse. It’s a strong supporting turn because the character’s fear is always visible under the loyalty.

lead_characters.name: Alicia Risaldi
lead_characters.demographics: Female, mid 50s, Victor’s wife, former stripper, mother of the Risaldi sons.
lead_characters.hook: Alicia is one of the script’s most painful casualties: a woman who has been reduced to status inside Victor’s worldview but still carries maternal feeling and fear. Her scenes make clear that she understands the family’s brutality and has learned to survive it by shrinking herself.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of bruised, tragic supporting role that can give an actor the same kind of devastating material Laura Linney or Patricia Clarkson often gets in prestige drama. It offers a chance to play humiliation, maternal terror, and quiet resistance.

lead_characters.name: Marcus Risaldi
lead_characters.hook: Marcus is the family’s moral test case, the child Victor fetishizes as innocent and uses as proof that purity can exist inside rot. He’s mostly a symbol on the page, but that symbol matters because the entire ending turns on whether he can be spared the family legacy.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: For a child performer, this is a high-visibility prestige role in the vein of the young actors in The Florida Project or Room — a part that carries emotional stakes without needing speeches. It’s the kind of role that can make a young actor memorable in a serious ensemble.

lead_characters.name: Lucy Winters
lead_characters.demographics: Female, early 30s, survivor of Victor’s abuse, married, mother.
lead_characters.hook: Lucy is one of the script’s clearest moral witnesses: a survivor who refuses to be defined by what happened to her and who names the system’s violence without flinching. Her scene with Jacob reframes the entire story by showing that the Risaldi damage extends far beyond the Smith family.
lead_characters.why_actor_wants_this: This is the kind of devastating survivor role that gives an actor the same kind of force Elisabeth Moss had in The Handmaid’s Tale or Jodie Comer in The Last Duel — controlled fury, trauma memory, and moral clarity. It’s a brief but potent showcase.

casting_characteristics: one child role with emotional significance
one late-30s female lead and one late-30s male lead-adjacent role
several roles require strong Catholic or working-class authenticity

notable_requirements: large mansion ballroom and private rooms

technical.vfx_details: No meaningful VFX beyond basic compositing and fire/smoke enhancement if desired.
technical.sfx_needs: Practical blood effects, gunshots, fire/smoke, body impacts, and destruction of evidence/warehouse materials.

rights_flags.detail: Come Back by The Five Stairsteps
Let All Mortal Flesh Keep Silent
500 Miles by Peter, Paul and Mary

platform_fit.series_engine_or_release_model: Feature release model: adult prestige crime drama with awards-friendly performance and thematic positioning.

budget.note: Contemporary and VFX-light, but the script wants a church, mansion, club, docks, police station, graveyard, apartment spaces, and multiple night exteriors with smoke/fire and crowd control. The scope is manageable, but the location count and night work will keep it above a lean contained-drama footprint.

casting.note: Jacob, Jodie, Ethan, and Victor all need actors who can carry moral intensity without flattening into genre types, and the Risaldi brothers need distinct energy rather than interchangeable heavies. Marcus and Lucy add age-specific and emotional specificity that narrows the search.

development.note: The script’s faith-and-violence thesis is distinctive, but the opening massacre, the family-tree density, and the repeated time jumps ask a buyer to track a lot of moving parts quickly. The material is strongest when the spiritual framework is clear, and that clarity has to hold across a dense ensemble.

comp_set.title: Manchester by the Sea
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-driven male lead carries unbearable loss with restraint, and the emotional payoff comes from how damage reshapes family relationships.

comp_set.title: Prisoners
comp_set.why_it_comps: The story shares the same punishing moral pressure, vigilante undertow, and bleak crime-world escalation around a devastated family.

comp_set.title: The Place Beyond the Pines
comp_set.why_it_comps: Intergenerational guilt, crime-family inheritance, and a fatalistic sense that violence is passed down like a curse.

comp_set.title: Wind River
comp_set.why_it_comps: A grief-fueled investigation, a morally burdened lead, and a cold, punitive atmosphere that turns the setting into part of the wound.

comp_set.title: Calvary
comp_set.why_it_comps: Catholic faith, confession, and moral reckoning are not background texture here; they’re the dramatic engine.

audience_target.primary_audience: Adults who respond to prestige crime dramas with spiritual or moral stakes, especially viewers drawn to grief, family collapse, and antihero punishment.
audience_target.demographics: 35-64, slightly male-skewing but viable for women who respond to elevated crime and family drama; educated, prestige-streaming audience.

budget_tier.note: Contemporary indie crime drama with a modest cast, practical violence, and multiple but scope-able locations; the main cost drivers are night work, crowd scenes, and the church/club/mansion/docks footprint.

lane_fit.detail: This sits naturally in the lane of elevated crime stories that sell on performance, moral tension, and a strong point of view rather than on spectacle. The Catholic framework and family-feud structure give it a clear identity for buyers looking for adult, awards-capable genre material.

ip_potential.detail: Standalone feature; the supporting characters are vivid, but the story resolves the Risaldi conflict as a closed moral and criminal cycle rather than opening a clean franchise or spinoff vector.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Catholic ritual gives the crime story a spine.
strengths.what_it_means: The confession booth, adoration chapel, hymns, and sermon structure give the film a distinctive identity that can help it stand out in a crowded crime-drama market. That makes it attractive to buyers who want elevated genre material with a clear thematic hook and to actors who want prestige dialogue scenes with emotional weight.
strengths.evidence: The repeated confession scenes, Father Michael’s sermons, and the way prayer and song recur around the violence.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Jacob is a grief role with real commercial weight.
strengths.what_it_means: The lead is built for a serious actor to anchor the film with pain, restraint, and eventual moral collapse, which is exactly the kind of performance that can elevate a mid-budget crime piece. That is the kind of role that attracts actor-driven financing and prestige-minded casting conversations.
strengths.evidence: Jacob’s therapy scene, the alley confrontation with Tyler, and the final ballroom breakdown.

strengths.dimension_or_area: The sibling dynamic gives the movie a second engine.
strengths.what_it_means: Jacob and Jodie are not just plot partners; they are emotionally opposed versions of survival, which gives the film recurring tension beyond the crime plot. That relationship broadens the audience appeal and gives the project a stronger emotional center for buyers and cast.
strengths.evidence: Their graveyard conversation, the apartment blowup, and the final reconciliation after Victor is cornered.

strengths.dimension_or_area: Victor is a clean, castable antagonist.
strengths.what_it_means: The father-patriarch role is sharply defined, easy to pitch, and loaded with scene work, which helps the project package around a veteran actor. A strong Victor can instantly communicate the movie’s threat level and prestige ambition.
strengths.evidence: The ballroom photo-ripping scene and the final confrontation where he frames murder as authority.

strengths.what_it_means: Police, church, docks, club, mansion, and public press all interact as one civic ecosystem, which gives the story texture and makes the city feel complicit. That density helps the film feel bigger than its budget and gives producers a clear sense of place.
strengths.evidence: The raids, press conferences, church vandalism, and public protests after the club fire.

whats_special.headline: This is a prestige crime drama with a real identity: Catholic ritual, family annihilation, and a grief-struck lead role that can carry the whole movie. It’s also producible in the indie lane, with practical violence and contained locations that let the script feel bigger than its budget.

items.detail: The script opens with a lot of names, time jumps, and family relationships before the central engine fully locks in. The massacre is memorable, but the buyer conversation will be about whether the audience can orient fast enough to stay emotionally attached through the first 10-15 pages.

items.area: Several Risaldi brothers read as variants of menace.
items.detail: Martin, Edward, Tyler, and Frankie each have a function, but not all of them have the same level of distinctiveness on the page. That matters because the family is the movie’s engine; if the brothers blur together, the emotional and strategic stakes flatten.

items.area: The violence level narrows the buyer pool.
items.detail: The child murder, repeated executions, and graphic family annihilation push the material into very mature territory. That is viable for premium streaming and some theatrical buyers, but it will immediately rule out a broader commercial lane.

items.area: The music and sermon material is clearance-heavy.
items.detail: The script names multiple songs — including Come Back, O Holy Night, 500 Miles, Clair de Lune, and L’Amour Toujours — and uses them as emotional punctuation. That creates real sync and budget planning, especially because the songs are not incidental background texture.

items.area: The final act depends on a very specific tonal balance.
items.detail: The ballroom climax has to hold rage, theology, family tragedy, and procedural payoff at once. That’s a strong ambition, but it also means the ending will be judged on whether the emotional catharsis lands cleanly rather than just violently.

issues.headline: The script’s biggest friction is orientation: the opening and the Risaldi family web ask the audience to do a lot of work before the emotional center fully settles. The other major conversation is market fit — this is a strong prestige play, but the violence and named music keep it in a narrower, adult-only lane.
